module_title: Scaling Broiler Production - From 200 to 5,000 Birds

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Assessing Your Readiness to Scale from 200 to 5,000 Birds
lessons.body: Scaling from 200 to 5,000 broilers is not simply multiplying everything by twenty-five. It is a fundamental shift in how you think about your farm, your money, your labour, and your market. Before you buy a single extra chick, you must honestly assess whether you are ready. Many African poultry farmers fail at this stage because they scale too fast, driven by a good season or a single large order. The result is overcrowded houses, disease outbreaks, feed shortages, and debt. This lesson helps you decide if you are truly ready. First, look at your current performance. If you cannot achieve a mortality rate below five percent and a feed conversion ratio of about 1.6 to 1.8 with 200 birds, you are not ready for 5,000. Scaling multiplies both your profits and your mistakes. Fix your basic management first. Track every bag of feed, every dead bird, every naira or shilling spent. If you do not keep records now, start today. A simple notebook is enough. Record chick cost, feed consumed, mortality, medication, labour, and sales. Without these numbers, you cannot know your true cost per bird. Second, assess your market. 5,000 birds will produce roughly 5,000 to 6,000 kilograms of live weight in six to eight weeks. Who will buy this? Do you have confirmed orders from hotels, restaurants, cold rooms, or market traders? Do not assume the market will absorb your birds just because you had no problem selling 200. Large buyers want consistent supply, uniform size, and reliable delivery. Visit potential buyers before you scale. Ask what size birds they prefer, how often they need them, and what price they pay. A written or verbal agreement, even informal, reduces risk. Third, examine your finances. Scaling requires serious capital. For 5,000 birds, you will need a house of at least 250 to 300 square metres, giving about 10 birds per square metre in hot climates or 12 in cooler areas. You will need feeders, drinkers, brooding equipment, feed for the entire cycle, vaccines, medication, labour, and a reserve for emergencies. In many African countries, the total cost per bird can range from 3 to 5 US dollars, meaning 5,000 birds could require 15,000 to 25,000 US dollars. Do you have this money, or can you access credit? Do not rely on selling birds to pay for the next batch of feed. That is a recipe for collapse. Fourth, evaluate your infrastructure. Can your current water supply handle 5,000 birds? A broiler drinks about 1.5 to 2 times its feed intake. In hot weather, water consumption can double. You need a reliable borehole, tank, or piped supply. Electricity is another issue. If you depend on a fridge for vaccines or a brooder for heat, you need a backup generator or solar system. Power cuts are common across Africa, and a failed brooder can kill thousands of chicks in hours. Fifth, think about labour. 200 birds can be managed by one person part-time. 5,000 birds need at least two full-time workers, plus extra help during catching and loading. You must train them in biosecurity, feeding, and spotting sick birds. Poorly trained staff are a major cause of disease spread. Sixth, consider your location. Are you near a major road? Can a truck reach your farm to deliver feed and collect birds? In rural areas, transport costs can eat your profit. Also, check local regulations. Some urban councils restrict poultry farming due to smell and waste. Make sure you are compliant. Finally, do a trial scale-up. Instead of jumping from 200 to 5,000, try 1,000 birds first. This allows you to test your systems, train your workers, and learn without risking everything. If you succeed with 1,000, then move to 2,500, then 5,000. This phased approach is used by successful commercial farmers across Africa. Remember, scaling is a business decision, not an emotional one. Be honest about your weaknesses. If you lack capital, start by partnering with a buyer who can advance you feed or chicks. If you lack land, consider renting a larger plot. If you lack knowledge, take a course or hire a consultant. The goal is not to have the biggest farm, but the most profitable and sustainable one. In the next lesson, we will look at housing and equipment for 5,000 birds.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Designing Housing and Equipment for 5,000 Broilers
lessons.body: When you move from 200 to 5,000 broilers, your housing and equipment must change dramatically. You cannot keep 5,000 birds in a small backyard pen. Overcrowding leads to poor growth, respiratory disease, cannibalism, and high mortality. This lesson gives practical, Africa-focused guidance on building or adapting a house for 5,000 birds, and on choosing the right equipment. First, calculate the space. The general rule for broilers in tropical Africa is 10 birds per square metre in open-sided houses, or 12 birds per square metre in controlled-environment houses with good ventilation. For 5,000 birds, you need at least 500 square metres of floor space if using 10 birds per square metre. That is a house 50 metres long and 10 metres wide. If you use 12 birds per square metre, you need about 417 square metres, for example 42 metres by 10 metres. Do not cut corners on space. Overcrowding is the number one cause of disease and poor feed conversion. Second, choose the right orientation. In hot climates, the house should run east to west, so the long sides face north and south. This reduces direct sunlight on the side walls and keeps the interior cooler. The roof should have a wide overhang, at least one metre, to shade the walls and prevent rain from entering. Use reflective roofing material, such as white or aluminium-coated iron sheets, to reduce heat absorption. In very hot areas, consider a double roof or a thatch layer over the iron sheets. Third, design for ventilation. Broilers generate a lot of heat and moisture. Without good airflow, ammonia from litter builds up and damages the birds' respiratory tracts. In open-sided houses, the sides should be open with wire mesh, but you can use curtains to control wind and rain. The ridge of the roof should have an opening for hot air to escape. If you are in a cooler highland area, you may need solid walls with adjustable vents. In all cases, air movement at bird level is critical. Use smoke tests or a simple anemometer to check airflow. Fourth, plan the floor and litter. The floor should be concrete or compacted earth, raised at least 30 centimetres above the surrounding ground to prevent flooding. Use wood shavings, rice husks, or chopped maize cobs as litter, spread 5 to 10 centimetres deep. Never use sawdust from treated wood, as it can be toxic. Litter must be dry and free of mould. Wet litter causes footpad dermatitis and respiratory problems. You will need to turn the litter regularly and add fresh material. Fifth, invest in proper feeders and drinkers. For 5,000 birds, manual feeding is possible but labour-intensive. A good option is tube feeders, one per 50 to 60 birds, meaning about 80 to 100 feeders. For drinkers, use bell drinkers, one per 80 to 100 birds, so about 50 to 60 drinkers. Alternatively, you can install an automatic nipple drinking system, which saves labour and keeps water cleaner. Nipple lines are more expensive upfront but reduce disease and water waste. If you use manual drinkers, clean them at least twice daily. Sixth, set up a reliable brooding area. For 5,000 chicks, you will need a brooder space of about 100 to 150 square metres for the first two weeks. You can brood in a section of the main house using cardboard or polythene curtains to confine the chicks. Provide supplementary heat using charcoal stoves, gas brooders, or infrared bulbs. In Africa, many farmers use charcoal or kerosene brooders, but these can cause carbon monoxide poisoning if ventilation is poor. Always ensure fresh air enters the brooding area. A simple rule: if you feel dizzy or smell fumes, the chicks are suffering. Seventh, consider feed storage. You will need to store several tonnes of feed at a time. A dry, raised store room with pallets to keep bags off the floor is essential. Rats and mice can eat or contaminate feed. Use metal bins or secure rooms. Do not store feed in the same room as birds, as it attracts pests and can spread disease. Eighth, plan for biosecurity. At the entrance of the house, have a footbath with disinfectant. Provide boots and overalls for workers. Limit visitors. If you have multiple houses, start with the youngest birds and work towards the oldest. Keep a record of all visitors. Ninth, think about waste management. 5,000 birds produce a lot of litter and manure. You can sell litter as fertiliser to crop farmers, or compost it. Do not dump it in waterways. A simple compost heap turned regularly will kill pathogens and produce good organic manure. Tenth, consider electricity and water backup. If you use automatic drinkers or brooders, you need a backup generator or solar system. A 5,000-bird farm can lose thousands of dollars if the power fails during a heatwave. Install a water tank of at least 2,000 litres and a pump. Finally, do not forget the catching and loading area. When selling, you need a place where birds can be caught easily and loaded onto a truck. A small holding pen near the road reduces stress and labour. In summary, housing for 5,000 broilers is a major investment. In many African countries, a simple open-sided house with wire mesh, iron sheets, and concrete floor can cost between 5,000 and 15,000 US dollars, depending on local prices. Equipment adds another 2,000 to 5,000 US dollars. Do not rush. Build in phases if necessary. A well-designed house will pay for itself through better growth, lower mortality, and higher profits. In the next lesson, we will cover feed and nutrition for large flocks.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Feed and Nutrition Management for 5,000 Broilers
lessons.body: Feed is the largest cost in broiler production, often representing 65 to 75 percent of total expenses. When you scale from 200 to 5,000 birds, feed management becomes a full-time job. Poor feed management leads to slow growth, high feed conversion ratios, and lost profit. This lesson provides practical, Africa-focused advice on feeding 5,000 broilers from day-old to market. First, understand the feed phases. Broilers need different nutrients at different ages. The typical phases are starter (0 to 10 days), grower (11 to 24 days), and finisher (25 days to market). Some farmers use a pre-starter for the first 5 days. Each phase has a different protein and energy level. Starter feed usually has 22 to 24 percent crude protein, grower 20 to 22 percent, and finisher 18 to 20 percent. Do not feed the wrong phase. Using finisher feed too early wastes protein and money; using starter feed too late slows growth and increases fat. Second, choose the right feed form. Mash is cheapest but causes waste and poor digestion. Pellets are more expensive but reduce waste and improve feed conversion. Crumbles are good for young chicks. In many African markets, you can buy commercial feed from reputable companies. If you mix your own feed, you must be very careful with ingredient quality and mixing. A common mistake is using poor-quality fishmeal or rancid oil, which causes disease and poor growth. If you mix your own, use a formula from a trusted extension officer or nutritionist. Third, calculate feed needs. A typical broiler eats about 4 to 4.5 kilograms of feed to reach 2.2 to 2.5 kilograms live weight in 6 to 7 weeks. For 5,000 birds, that is 20,000 to 22,500 kilograms of feed per cycle, or 20 to 22.5 tonnes. You need to plan your purchases and storage. Buying in bulk reduces cost. A 50-kilogram bag of commercial broiler feed in many African countries costs between 25 and 40 US dollars, depending on the country and quality. For 5,000 birds, your total feed bill could be 10,000 to 18,000 US dollars per cycle. This is a huge investment. You must have the money or credit before you start. Fourth, set up a feeding schedule. Chicks need feed available at all times for the first two weeks. Use shallow trays or chick feeders for the first few days, then switch to tube feeders. From week three, you can feed twice daily, but many farmers prefer ad libitum feeding, meaning feed is always available. However, ad libitum can lead to waste if feeders are not managed. Fill feeders to one-third capacity to reduce spillage. Adjust feeder height so the lip is at the level of the birds' backs. This reduces scratching and waste. Fifth, manage water. Water is often overlooked. Broilers need clean, fresh water at all times. A bird drinks about 1.5 to 2 times its feed intake by weight. In hot weather, water intake can double. For 5,000 birds, you need a reliable water supply of at least 1,000 to 2,000 litres per day. If you use manual drinkers, clean them twice daily. If you use nipple drinkers, check the pressure and clean the lines regularly. Add electrolytes or vitamins to water during heat stress or after vaccination. Never add medication to water without veterinary advice. Sixth, monitor feed conversion ratio (FCR). FCR is the amount of feed eaten divided by the weight gained. A good FCR for broilers is 1.6 to 1.8. If your FCR is above 2.0, you are losing money. To calculate FCR, weigh a sample of birds weekly and record feed consumed. If FCR is poor, check for disease, poor feed quality, overcrowding, or feed waste. Seventh, reduce feed waste. Feed waste can be 5 to 10 percent if feeders are poorly designed or overfilled. Use feeders with lips to prevent birds from scooping feed out. Do not fill feeders more than half full. Repair holes in bags. Store feed on pallets in a dry room. Keep rodents out. Eighth, consider alternative feed ingredients. In Africa, commercial feed is expensive. Some farmers use locally available ingredients like maize, soybean meal, fishmeal, and sunflower cake. However, mixing your own feed requires careful balancing of energy, protein, vitamins, and minerals. A common mistake is using too much maize, which lowers protein. If you want to mix your own feed, work with a nutritionist. Also, consider using feed additives like enzymes or probiotics, which can improve digestion and reduce disease. Ninth, plan for feed storage. You will need a store room that is dry, ventilated, and rat-proof. Bags should be stacked on pallets at least 10 centimetres off the floor and 30 centimetres away from walls. Do not stack more than 10 bags high, as the bottom bags can become compacted and mouldy. Use older feed first. Never use mouldy feed. Aflatoxin from mouldy maize or groundnuts can kill birds and leave residues in meat. Tenth, budget for feed price fluctuations. In many African countries, feed prices rise during the dry season or when maize harvests are poor. Buy in bulk when prices are low if you have storage. Some farmers form cooperatives to buy feed together and get discounts. Finally, keep records. Record the date, amount, and type of feed given to each flock. This helps you calculate FCR, cost per bird, and profit. Without records, you cannot know if you are making money. In summary, feeding 5,000 broilers is a serious business. You must buy quality feed, store it well, feed correctly, and monitor performance. A well-fed flock will reward you with fast growth and high profit. In the next lesson, we will cover health and biosecurity for large flocks.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Health and Biosecurity for 5,000 Broilers
lessons.body: When you keep 5,000 broilers, disease is your biggest threat. A single outbreak of Newcastle disease or avian influenza can wipe out your entire flock and your investment. Biosecurity is not optional; it is the foundation of successful large-scale broiler production. This lesson provides practical, Africa-focused steps to keep your birds healthy. First, understand the common diseases. In Africa, the most devastating broiler diseases include Newcastle disease, infectious bursal disease (Gumboro), avian influenza, fowl pox, coccidiosis, and chronic respiratory disease. Newcastle and Gumboro are viral and have no cure; you must vaccinate. Coccidiosis is caused by a parasite and is treated with anticoccidials. Chronic respiratory disease is often caused by poor ventilation and ammonia. Avian influenza is a deadly zoonotic disease; report suspected cases immediately to veterinary authorities. Second, establish a vaccination programme. Work with a local veterinarian to design a schedule. A typical programme for broilers in Africa includes: day 1, Marek's disease vaccine (often given at hatchery); day 7, Newcastle disease and infectious bronchitis; day 14, Gumboro; day 21, Newcastle booster; and day 28, Gumboro booster. Some farms also vaccinate against fowl pox at day 21. Vaccines must be stored correctly. Most need refrigeration at 2 to 8 degrees Celsius. Never freeze vaccines. Use clean water for drinking water vaccines and add skimmed milk powder to neutralise chlorine. Vaccinate early in the morning or late evening to reduce heat stress. Third, implement strict biosecurity. Biosecurity means keeping pathogens out. The key steps are: limit visitors; use footbaths with fresh disinfectant at every entrance; provide boots and overalls for workers; wash hands before entering; keep different age groups separate; do not mix birds from different sources; and control rodents, wild birds, and insects. In Africa, many farms fail because workers move between farms or bring contaminated clothes. Pay your workers well and train them. A simple rule: if you visit another farm, do not enter your own house for at least 24 hours, or change clothes and shower. Fourth, manage litter and ventilation. Wet litter and poor ventilation cause respiratory disease and coccidiosis. Keep litter dry by fixing water leaks immediately. Stir litter daily. Increase ventilation to remove ammonia. Ammonia levels above 20 parts per million damage the respiratory tract. You can smell ammonia when it is above 20 ppm. If your eyes water when you enter the house, the level is too high. Fifth, use a good coccidiostat. Coccidiosis is common in deep litter systems. Many commercial feeds contain a coccidiostat. If you mix your own feed, add a coccidiostat according to veterinary advice. Do not use the same coccidiostat continuously; rotate to prevent resistance. Sixth, monitor your birds daily. Walk through the flock at least twice a day. Look for sick birds: those that are dull, huddling, panting, or have diarrhoea. Remove sick birds immediately and isolate them. If many birds are sick, call a veterinarian. Do not guess. Post-mortem examination of dead birds can reveal the cause. Seventh, keep records of mortality. A mortality rate of 5 percent or less is good. If mortality rises above 1 percent per week, investigate. Common causes include poor quality chicks, disease, heat stress, or starvation. Record daily deaths and note any patterns. Eighth, control heat stress. Broilers are very sensitive to heat. In hot African climates, heat stress can kill thousands of birds in a single afternoon. Provide shade, increase ventilation, use fans, and wet the roof or walls. Add electrolytes to water. Feed during the coolest parts of the day. Never overcrowd. Ninth, handle dead birds properly. Dead birds must be disposed of immediately. Use incineration, deep burial, or composting. Do not sell or eat dead birds. Do not throw them into rivers or bushes. This spreads disease. Tenth, plan for disease outbreaks. Have a contingency plan. Keep a reserve of money for veterinary care. Know the contact of a good vet. If you suspect avian influenza, do not move birds. Call authorities. Finally, remember that prevention is cheaper than treatment. A healthy flock grows faster and costs less. Vaccines, biosecurity, and good management are your best investments. In the next lesson, we will cover marketing and selling 5,000 broilers.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Marketing and Selling 5,000 Broilers Profitably
lessons.body: Producing 5,000 broilers is only half the battle. Selling them profitably is the other half. Many African farmers fail at this stage because they have no market plan. They produce birds and then look for buyers, often selling at low prices or losing birds to spoilage. This lesson provides practical, Africa-focused strategies for marketing and selling 5,000 broilers. First, understand your market. There are several types of buyers: live bird traders, hotels and restaurants, cold rooms and butcheries, supermarkets, and individual consumers. Each has different needs. Live bird traders buy in bulk but pay lower prices. Hotels and restaurants pay higher prices but demand consistent size, quality, and regular supply. Cold rooms and butcheries want processed, chilled birds. Supermarkets require strict standards, packaging, and certifications. Individual consumers buy small numbers but pay retail prices. You must decide which market you will target. For 5,000 birds, you cannot rely on individual consumers alone. You need at least two or three bulk buyers. Second, do market research before you start. Visit local markets, hotels, and cold rooms. Ask what price they pay, what size birds they prefer, and how often they need supply. In many African countries, broilers are sold live, but demand for processed chicken is growing. If you can process and package birds, you can earn more. However, processing requires investment in a slaughter area, cold storage, and packaging. Third, set a competitive price. Calculate your cost per bird. Include chick cost, feed, medication, labour, housing depreciation, and transport. Add a profit margin of 20 to 30 percent. Check the market price. If your cost is higher than the market price, you cannot compete. You must reduce costs or find a premium market. For example, organic or free-range chicken sells at a higher price in some cities. Fourth, plan your sales schedule. Do not sell all 5,000 birds at once. The market may be flooded, and prices will drop. Sell in batches. For example, sell 1,000 birds per week over five weeks. This keeps prices stable and gives you time to find buyers. However, you must manage feed and space carefully. If you hold birds longer than 8 weeks, feed conversion worsens, and you lose money. Fifth, build relationships with buyers. Trust is key. Deliver on time. Provide consistent size and quality. If you promise 1,500 birds every Friday, do not miss a delivery. Buyers will pay more for reliability. Offer a small discount for bulk orders or repeat customers. Use a simple contract or written agreement, even if informal. Sixth, consider processing. Live birds are cheaper to sell but have a lower price. Processed birds, including slaughtered, plucked, and eviscerated, sell for 30 to 50 percent more. You can process on-farm or use a local abattoir. If you process, you need a clean area, sharp knives, a plucking machine or manual plucking, and cold storage. In many African countries, you can sell processed chicken to hotels, restaurants, and supermarkets. You can also sell parts: breasts, thighs, wings, and drumsticks. This adds value. Seventh, use marketing and promotion. In the digital age, use WhatsApp, Facebook, and local radio to advertise. Take photos of your healthy birds and clean facilities. Offer free samples to hotel chefs. Attend local agricultural shows. Create a simple brand name. Word of mouth is powerful. Satisfied customers will refer others. Eighth, manage transport and logistics. You need a reliable way to deliver birds. Live birds can be transported in crates. Processed birds need a cold chain. If you do not have a refrigerated truck, use insulated boxes with ice. Plan your route to minimise stress on birds and time. In rural areas, poor roads can cause delays and mortality. Ninth, handle payments carefully. Do not sell on credit unless you trust the buyer. Many farmers have lost money to buyers who promise to pay later. If you must offer credit, take a deposit of at least 50 percent. Use mobile money for secure payments. Keep records of all sales. Tenth, deal with surplus and low demand. If you cannot sell all birds, you can freeze them. Invest in a chest freezer or rent cold storage. You can also dry or smoke meat for longer shelf life. In some areas, you can sell to school feeding programmes or government institutions. Finally, calculate your profit. At the end of the cycle, subtract all costs from total sales. If you made a profit, reinvest part of it and save part. If you made a loss, find out why. Was it feed cost, mortality, or low price? Adjust for the next cycle. Successful broiler farming is a cycle of continuous improvement. In summary, marketing is not an afterthought. It is a core part of your business. Plan your market before you buy chicks. Build relationships, deliver quality, and manage your money well. With 5,000 birds, you can build a thriving business that supports your family and creates jobs in your community.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Scaling to 5,000 Broilers in Africa â Numbers, Benchmarks and Decision Tools

This lesson is a working reference. It does not teach new concepts â it gives you the figures, thresholds and checklists you need when you are standing in the poultry house at 6 a.m. with 5,000 birds looking at you, or sitting with a bank officer who wants to know whether your enterprise can service a loan. Every number here is drawn from published official sources, with the source named so you can verify it yourself. Use it as a laminated sheet on the wall of the feed store, not as bedtime reading.

The business logic is simple: at 200 birds you can absorb mistakes with your own labour and a little cash. At 5,000 birds, a 5% mortality spike, a two-day feed delay, or a 100 g shortfall in average daily gain translates directly into tens of thousands of shillings of lost margin. Precision is no longer a virtue â it is the difference between profit and debt.

Table 1: Performance and Cost Benchmarks for 5,000 Broilers (Tropical Africa)

Cumulative mortality to day 42 â¤ 5% 3â8% FAO / MSD Animal Health poultry guidance

How to use Table 1: Weigh 5% of your flock weekly. If average weight is more than 10% below the target at day 21 or day 35, check feed quality, water access, and disease before blaming the genetics. If FCR exceeds 2.0, your feed is being wasted â look for spillage, rodent loss, or poor gut health.

Table 2: Input Requirements and Cash Flow per 5,000-Bird Cycle

Input / Line Item Quantity for 5,000 Birds Notes & Source

Cash flow warning: Feed alone for 5,000 birds is roughly 21.5 tonnes. If you cannot secure and store that volume before day 1, do not start the cycle. Running out of feed at week 4 is the single most common cause of failed scaling attempts in African broiler enterprises.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â HEALTH, VACCINES AND CHEMICALS

Vaccines and veterinary chemicals used in broiler production can harm you, your workers and your birds if handled incorrectly. Observe the following at all times:

  • Vaccines: Store at 2â8 Â°C. Never freeze. Use reconstituted vaccines within 2 hours. Dispose of vials and needles in a sharps container â never in household waste.
  • Antibiotics and coccidiostats: Use only under veterinary prescription. Respect withdrawal periods before slaughter â failure to do so leaves drug residues in meat and can cost you your market licence.
  • Disinfectants: Wear gloves and eye protection. Never mix different chemicals. Store away from feed and children.
  • Dead bird disposal: Bury at least 1 m deep or incinerate. Never feed dead birds to other animals â this spreads disease.
  • Personal hygiene: Wash hands after handling birds, litter or chemicals. Change boots and clothing between houses.

Sources: WHO guidance on antimicrobial resistance in food animals; MSD Animal Health poultry vaccination protocols; FAO biosecurity guidelines.

Quick Reference Checklist â Before You Start a 5,000-Bird Cycle

  1. Cash secured: You have enough money to buy all feed, chicks, vaccines and pay labour for 8 weeks â not just for week 1.
  2. Housing ready: 400â500 mÂ² of clean, dry, disinfected floor space with working ventilation and water lines tested at full pressure.
  3. Feed contract signed: A written supply agreement for 21.5 tonnes of feed, with delivery dates and quality specifications.
  4. Vet visit done: A registered veterinarian has reviewed your biosecurity plan and vaccination schedule for your district.
  5. Water tested: Water is clean and available at 40,000+ litres for the cycle; tanks and lines cleaned and flushed.
  6. Market confirmed: You have at least two buyers who have agreed on price range, volume and collection date before day 42.
  7. Records system ready: A simple notebook or app for daily feed, water, mortality, weight and medication records.
  8. Contingency plan: You know what you will do if mortality exceeds 2% in week 1, or if feed prices rise 20% mid-cycle.

Further Reading â Free Official Resources

  • FAO â Poultry Production and Products: global guidance on smallholder and commercial poultry production, housing and biosecurity.
  • Aviagen â Ross 308 Broiler Performance Objectives: the definitive free reference for growth, FCR and feed intake targets.
  • ILRI â Livestock Value Chains: research on smallholder poultry economics and market access in East and West Africa.
  • MSD Animal Health â Poultry: vaccination schedules, disease prevention and biosecurity protocols.
  • WHO â Antimicrobial Resistance Fact Sheet: why responsible drug use in poultry matters for human health and market access.

Final business note: Print Table 1 and Table 2. Tape them inside your feed store door. Weigh your birds every Sunday. Write down every bag of feed that enters the house. The farmers who scale successfully from 200 to 5,000 birds are not the ones with the best genetics â they are the ones who measure, record and act on the numbers in this lesson.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of the brooding period in broiler production?
options: B) To provide heat and care for young chicks
D) To prepare birds for transport
quiz.explanation: The brooding period provides supplemental heat, water, feed, and care to help young chicks survive and grow during their first days of life.

quiz.q: Which environmental factor is most critical to monitor during brooding?
options: A) Wind speed outside the house
D) Number of workers on the farm
quiz.explanation: Chick-level temperature directly affects comfort, feed intake, and survival, so it is the most critical brooding factor to monitor.

quiz.q: What does a high feed conversion ratio indicate in broiler production?
options: C) Feed is being wasted or birds are less efficient
D) Water intake is too low
quiz.explanation: A high feed conversion ratio means more feed is required per unit of weight gain, indicating poorer efficiency or waste.

quiz.q: Which ventilation strategy helps remove moisture and ammonia from a broiler house?
options: D) Minimum ventilation with controlled air exchange
Minimum ventilation exchanges stale air with fresh air to remove moisture
and carbon dioxide while conserving heat.

quiz.q: What is the recommended action when chicks are panting and spreading away from heat sources?
options: A) Lower the brooding temperature or increase ventilation
quiz.explanation: Panting and spreading away from heat indicate overheating, so temperature should be reduced or ventilation improved.

quiz.q: Why is uniform bird size important at market age in broiler production?
options: B) It improves processing efficiency and product consistency
C) It eliminates the need for vaccination
quiz.explanation: Uniform flocks are easier to process, meet market specifications better, and produce more consistent end products.

quiz.q: Which practice best helps prevent footpad dermatitis in broilers?
quiz.explanation: Dry, well-managed litter reduces contact with moisture and ammonia, which are major causes of footpad dermatitis.

quiz.q: What is a key reason to record daily mortality in a broiler flock?
options: C) To decide feed formulation only
D) To detect health or management problems early
Daily mortality records help producers identify disease
or management issues before they cause major losses.
